mainTopic: Testing whether הילך is exempt from a שבועה, using a ברייתא about an unnumbered שטר and a משנה about claims of vessels and land.
overview: The גמרא continues its question of whether a defendant who says הֵילָךְ ('here you are') is exempt from a שבועה. It brings a ברייתא about a שטר that says only 'סלעים' or 'דינרין', which proves at least two. The lender claims five and the borrower admits three. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says he swears as a מודה במקצת, and רבי עקיבא says he is like a מֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה and is פטור. The גמרא first tries to prove from רבי שמעון בן אלעזר that הילך פטור. It ends up saying that admitting two is פטור only because the שטר backs the borrower up, or because a שטר creates a lien on land and no oath is taken over land. A second version reads רבי עקיבא to prove the opposite, that הילך חייב. The גמרא shows by logic that רבי עקיבא exempts even someone who admits two, and that this still does not refute רבי חייא. Finally מר זוטרא tries to prove הילך חייב from a משנה about claims of vessels and land. The גמרא answers that the land case was chosen to teach זוקקין, an oath on movables pulling in the land, and that שבועות, not קידושין, is that rule's main home.

steps.title: The ברייתא: a שטר with no number written
steps.stepSummary: A שטר says 'סלעים' or 'דינרין' with no number. The lender claims five and the borrower admits three. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says the borrower swears as a מודה במקצת. רבי עקיבא says he is like a מֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה and is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a שטר says 'סלעים' or 'דינרין', and the lender says five while the borrower says three: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says that since he admitted part of the claim, he must swear. רבי עקיבא says he is only like someone returning a lost object, and he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the rest of a ברייתא that it will use as a test case. This step lays out the case and the מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plural word like 'סלעים' proves at least two, so the שטר already obligates the borrower for two. רבי עקיבא holds that admitting the third is a voluntary, honest admission, like returning a lost object, so no שבועה is needed. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר treats the borrower as a regular מודה במקצת who must swear on the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: The lender
The borrower
He admitted part of the claim, which normally obligates a שבועה
He must swear
One who returns a lost object; an honest volunteer who is exempt from swearing

steps.confusionAlert: Where do the 'two' come from? A plural word like 'סלעים' or 'דינרין' means at least two. So the שטר already proves two, and the argument is only about the coins beyond that.

phrases.english: Sela'im, dinars.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא is about a שטר that just says 'sela'im' or 'dinars' with no number, which means at least two.

phrases.english: The lender says five,
and the borrower says three.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Since he admitted part of the claim, he must swear.
Rabbi Akiva says:
He is only like one who returns a lost object, and he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַלְוֶה אוֹמֵר חָמֵשׁ, וְלֹוֶה אוֹמֵר שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא the גמרא began quoting just before, as part of its inquiry into הילך.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: the borrower who admits three swears as a מודה במקצת. רבי עקיבא: he is like a מֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה and is פטור.

steps.title: Proof from the ברייתא that הילך is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads רבי שמעון בן אלעזר closely. He requires a שבועה only because the borrower admitted three. That implies admitting two would be פטור, because the two in the שטר count as הילך. So הילך פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא teaches that רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says the borrower swears because he admitted part of the claim. The reason is that he said three. But if he had said two, he would be exempt. The two in the שטר that he admits to count as 'here you are'. Learn from this that 'here you are' is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove from the ברייתא that a defendant who says הֵילָךְ is exempt from a שבועה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case specifically says 'three', which suggests that admitting only two would not obligate a שבועה. The two are already secured by the שטר, so admitting them is like handing them over on the spot (הילך). If such an admission doesn't trigger a שבועה, then הילך פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches; focuses on one part of a source
The reason is; often sets up an inference from the opposite case
'Here you are': the defendant is handing over the part he admits right now
Learn from it; announces a proof
A written document, here a loan document

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a real attempt to settle whether הילך פטור, which decides when a partial admission triggers a שבועה.

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says,
since he admitted part of the claim, he must swear.
The reason is that he said three,
but if he said two, he would be exempt,
and this שטר that he admits to
is 'here you are',
phrases.notes: The two coins the שטר already proves are treated as if he were handing them over right now.

phrases.english: so learn from it that 'here you are' is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the wording of the ברייתא quoted in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That הילך פטור: a defendant who hands over the admitted portion is not obligated to swear.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's case of 'three' under רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, implying that admitting only the two secured by the שטר is פטור.

steps.title: Rejection: 'three' is only there to argue against רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that even admitting two might obligate a שבועה. The ברייתא says 'three' only to argue against רבי עקיבא, who calls this borrower a מֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר teaches that he is a regular מודה במקצת and must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. I can tell you that even if he said two, he is obligated. The ברייתא says three only to argue against רבי עקיבא, who says he is like someone returning a lost object and is exempt. It teaches us that he counts as admitting part of the claim, and he is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by giving a different reason why the ברייתא mentions 'three'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depended on reading 'three' as excluding 'two'. The גמרא says 'three' was chosen because that is the case where רבי עקיבא exempts him, so it is just the point of argument. It says nothing about two, so no proof for הילך פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, I can tell you; introduces a rejection
Obligated (here, to swear)
To exclude; to argue against a different view
It teaches us

phrases.english: No, actually I can tell you
that with two he is obligated,
and the reason it teaches three
is to exclude the view of Rabbi Akiva,
who says: he is like one returning a lost object, and exempt;
it teaches us
that he counts as admitting part of the claim, and he is obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 2 by reading the word 'three' differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the inference that 'three' excludes 'two'; it does not prove the opposite about הילך.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'Three' is mentioned to argue against רבי עקיבא, not to exclude a case of two.

steps.title: Challenge: then it should have said 'even this one swears'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rejection. If even admitting two obligates a שבועה, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר should have said 'אַף זֶה יִשָּׁבַע', 'even this one swears'. His plain wording suggests he is giving the reason for the שבועה, not adding to an obvious case.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then instead of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר saying 'since he admitted part of the claim, he swears', he should have said 'even this one swears'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rejection from step 3 by pointing to the exact wording of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. The next step responds by dropping step 3's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If admitting two already obligates a שבועה, then three is obviously included, and the natural wording would be 'even this one swears'. Instead, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר gives a reason: 'since he admitted part of the claim'. That sounds like three is the case that creates the obligation, which brings back the proof that הילך פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; introduces a challenge based on the previous answer
Even this one
He should have said

phrases.english: If so:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
'Since he admitted part of the claim, he swears'?
He should have said 'even this one swears'!
phrases.notes: 'Even this one' would mean 'on top of the person who admits two'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection of step 3 using the exact wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 3 that admitting two also obligates a שבועה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If two already obligates a שבועה, three is obviously included and should be phrased 'אַף זֶה יִשָּׁבַע'. Giving a reason instead ('הוֹאִיל וְהוֹדָה') implies three is the case that creates the obligation.

steps.title: Two is exempt, but only because the document backs him up
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now accepts that admitting two is פטור. It explains that this is because the שטר supports the borrower, not because הילך is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, really, admitting two is exempt, and 'here you are' in general is obligated. This case is different, because the document supports him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its earlier answer from Step 3 and gives a new way to block the proof from Step 2. It agrees that two is פטור here, but says the reason is special to this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 argued: admitting two is פטור, and the two are like הילך, so הילך must be פטור. The גמרא now keeps the first half and cuts the link to הילך. The borrower is פטור because the שטר itself backs up his position, so this case teaches nothing about הילך in general.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Here you are.' The defendant admits part of the claim and hands over that part right away.
'Really' or 'actually.' The גמרא is giving the true reading.
'Here it is different.' This case has a special feature.
'Supports him.' Something backs up his side.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is now saying הילך is פטור. It says the opposite: in general הילך is חייב. Only this שטר case is פטור, for its own special reason.

phrases.english: Rather: really, admitting two is exempt,
and 'here you are' is obligated.
But here it is different,
because the document supports him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: לְעוֹלָם שְׁתַּיִם פָּטוּר, וְהֵילָךְ חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 4, replaces the answer of Step 3, and blocks the proof of Step 2 in a new way.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that הילך is פטור, while agreeing that admitting two is פטור.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The exemption comes from the שטר supporting the borrower, not from a general rule of הילך.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the pattern for the rest of the section: a case may be פטור for its own special reason, so it cannot prove a general rule.

steps.title: A second reason: a document creates a lien on land
steps.stepSummary: Another reason admitting two is פטור: a שטר places a lien on the borrower's land, and there is no שבועה on denying a debt secured by land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Alternatively, because it is a document with a lien on land, and one does not swear about a denial of a lien on land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different reason why admitting two is פטור here. This again shows the case does not prove that הילך is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan written in a שטר is tied to the borrower's land, and the rule is that oaths are not given about land. So the borrower's denial of the rest is a denial about land, and no שבועה applies. Again the exemption has nothing to do with הילך.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Alternatively.' Here comes a second possible answer.
A lien on land. The lender can collect from the borrower's property.
Denial. The defendant says he does not owe.
'One does not swear.' No court oath is given.

phrases.english: Alternatively: because it is
a document that creates a lien on land,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל כְּפִירַת שִׁעְבּוּד קַרְקָעוֹת.
phrases.english: and one does not swear over a denial of a lien on land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ שְׁטָר שִׁעְבּוּד קַרְקָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent reason, alongside Step 5, for why two is פטור without proving anything about הילך.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that הילך is פטור.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The exemption comes from the rule that no oath is given on land liens, not from הילך.

steps.title: From רבי עקיבא's words: maybe 'here you are' is obligated
steps.stepSummary: A second version of the sugya reads רבי עקיבא closely. He exempts the borrower who says three, which suggests two would be חייב. Since the two in the שטר are like הילך, this would prove הילך is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some object from the end of the ברייתא: רבי עקיבא says he is just like one who returns a lost item and is exempt. The reason is that he said three. But if he said two, he would be obligated. And the document, since he admits it, is like 'here you are.' Learn from this that 'here you are' is obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different version of the discussion. This time the inference is drawn from the end of the ברייתא, רבי עקיבא's opinion, and it points to the opposite result: הילך is חייב. That is a challenge to the view that הילך is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא calls the borrower who admits three a מֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה, because he admitted more than he had to. That suggests a borrower who admits only two, which he had to admit anyway because of the שטר, gets no such credit and must swear. Since those two count as הילך, הילך would be חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: 'There are those who object.' A second version of the discussion begins.
The later part of a teaching, here רבי עקיבא's opinion.
One who returns a lost item. He is honest by choice, so we do not make him swear.
'Learn from it.' This introduces the proof's conclusion.

steps.confusionAlert: Step 2 read רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and tried to prove הילך is פטור. This step reads רבי עקיבא and tries to prove the reverse, that הילך is חייב. Same ברייתא, opposite direction.

phrases.english: There are those who object from the later part:
phrases.notes: This is a different version of the same discussion, not a continuation of Steps 5 and 6.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
He is only like one who returns a lost item, and is exempt.
The reason is that he said three,
but if he said two, he would be obligated.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא שְׁטָר, כֵּיוָן דְּקָא מוֹדֵי בֵּיהּ
phrases.english: And this document, since he admits to it,
is like 'here you are.'
phrases.notes: He means the two the שטר already proves. Admitting them is like handing them over.

phrases.english: Learn from this that 'here you are' is obligated!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second version of the discussion, drawing an inference from the end of the ברייתא instead of the beginning.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that הילך is פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי עקיבא's focus on three implies two is חייב. The two in the שטר are like הילך, so הילך is חייב.

steps.title: 'Three' is said only to argue with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי עקיבא would exempt even someone who admits two. The ברייתא says 'three' only so that רבי עקיבא can argue against רבי שמעון בן אלעזר in the same case.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really I will tell you that two is also exempt. The reason the ברייתא says three is to reject רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, who says he is one who admits part of the claim and is obligated. רבי עקיבא teaches us that he is one who returns a lost item and is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof of Step 7. It explains why רבי עקיבא's words mention 'three' even though two would also be פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'three' does not show that two is חייב. It was chosen because that is the case where רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says the borrower must swear. רבי עקיבא answers him in that same case, so nothing can be learned about two, and nothing about הילך. This mirrors the move in Step 3, now on רבי עקיבא's side.

keyTerms.meaning: 'To exclude.' The wording is chosen to reject another opinion.
'He teaches us.' This is the new point being made.
One who admits part of the claim. He must take a תורה oath.

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides of the ברייתא were tested: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's words to prove הילך is פטור, and רבי עקיבא's words to prove הילך is חייב. Each proof is blocked. The number 'three' may be there only because of the argument, or the case may be פטור for a special reason such as the שטר or the land lien. So this ברייתא does not settle the law of הילך.

phrases.english: No, really I will tell you
that admitting two is also exempt,
and the reason it teaches three
is to exclude the view of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר מוֹדֶה מִקְצָת הַטַּעֲנָה הָוֵי – וְחַיָּיב,
phrases.english: who says he is one who admits part of the claim, and is obligated;

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּמֵשִׁיב אֲבֵידָה הָוֵי – וּפָטוּר.
phrases.english: so he teaches us that he is one who returns a lost item, and is exempt.
phrases.notes: The 'he' who teaches us here is רבי עקיבא.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ שְׁתַּיִם נָמֵי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of Step 7 by explaining why the number 'three' appears.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference that two is חייב according to רבי עקיבא, and with it the proof that הילך is חייב.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The number 'three' was chosen to match the case of the argument with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, not to exclude the case of two.

steps.title: Logic shows that admitting two must also be exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the last answer. If admitting two required a שבועה, רבי עקיבא could not exempt the borrower who says three, because he could just be using a trick.
steps.simpleTranslation: This makes sense. If admitting two required an oath, how could רבי עקיבא exempt someone who admits three? That person might be playing a trick. He could think: 'If I say two, I have to swear. So I'll say three, and then I'm like someone returning a lost object, and I'm free.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings logical support for the answer in step 8, that רבי עקיבא exempts even someone who admits two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose admitting two required a שבועה. Then a borrower could easily escape the oath by inflating his admission to three. In that case רבי עקיבא's reason for exempting him, that he is like someone returning a lost object, would fall apart, since he might be a schemer rather than an honest man.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is logical: this phrase brings support for what was just said
He is acting with trickery
One who returns a lost object; he is trusted and does not swear

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable.
For if it would enter your mind
that one who admits two is obligated to swear,

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁלֹשׁ הֵיכִי פָּטַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
phrases.english: then with three, how could Rabbi Akiva exempt him?
This one is just using a trick!
He thinks: If I say two,
I will need to swear.
So let me say three,
so that I will be like one returning a lost object, and I'll be exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings logical support for step 8's answer about רבי עקיבא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא exempts even someone who admits two.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Reasoning: if two were חייב, exempting three would reward a trick.

steps.title: Conclusion: admitting two is also exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that in רבי עקיבא's view, admitting two is also פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: So learn from this: admitting two is also exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the conclusion of the logic in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the trick would make the ruling of three meaningless, admitting two must also be פטור. This means the reading of רבי עקיבא in step 7 cannot be used to prove that הילך is חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: this phrase draws a conclusion

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי עקיבא, a borrower who admits the two written in the שטר and denies the rest does not swear. Saying three was just the case the ברייתא happened to discuss.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from it:
admitting two is also exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: שְׁתַּיִם נָמֵי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof begun in step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For רבי עקיבא, admitting two is פטור, so his ruling does not prove that הילך is חייב.

steps.title: This seems to be a problem for רבי חייא
steps.stepSummary: If admitting two is exempt, that looks like a case of הילך being פטור, which goes against רבי חייא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then this is difficult for רבי חייא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the conclusion around and asks how רבי חייא, who holds that הילך is חייב, can explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two dinars proven by the שטר are like הילך, since the lender can already collect them through the document. If admitting them gives no שבועה, that seems to show הילך is פטור, which contradicts רבי חייא.

keyTerms.meaning: It is difficult for רבי חייא

phrases.english: But this is difficult for Rabbi Chiya!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the conclusion of step 10 to attack רבי חייא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's view that הילך is חייב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two in the שטר are like הילך, and they are exempt, so הילך should be פטור.

steps.title: The שטר supports the borrower
steps.stepSummary: The answer for רבי חייא: this case is different because the שטר backs up the borrower's claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the note supports him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי חייא, using the same reason it gave in step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption is not because of הילך. The שטר proves no more than two, so it backs up the borrower's denial of anything beyond that, and that is why he does not swear. רבי חייא's rule about הילך stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
The document supports him

phrases.english: It is different there,
because the note supports him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם דְּקָא מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ שְׁטָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge to רבי חייא in step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exemption comes from הילך, which goes against רבי חייא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption comes from the שטר's support, so הילך can still be חייב.

steps.title: A land-backed debt carries no oath
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: a שטר creates a lien on land, and no שבועה is taken on denying a debt backed by land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else, because it is a note that puts a lien on land, and we do not swear about denying a lien on land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer for רבי חייא, the same reason it gave in step 6.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land, and claims tied to land, are never subject to this kind of שבועה. A debt written in a שטר is secured by the borrower's land, so denying it brings no oath at all. Again, this has nothing to do with הילך.

keyTerms.meaning: A lien on land: the lender can collect from the borrower's property
Denial of a claim
Alternatively: this introduces a second answer

phrases.english: Alternatively, because it is
a note that creates a lien on land,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל כְּפִירַת שִׁעְבּוּד קַרְקָעוֹת.
phrases.english: and we do not swear over denying a lien on land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ שְׁטָר שִׁעְבּוּד קַרְקָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exemption is because of הילך.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption is because land-backed debts carry no שבועה.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי חייא survives: the exemption in the שטר case comes from the שטר itself (its support or its lien on land), not from הילך.

steps.title: מר זוטרא quotes a משנה about vessels and land
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא raises an objection by quoting a משנה about claims of vessels and land, and which admissions require a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא son of רב נחמן objected: If someone claimed vessels and land from another person, and the other admitted the vessels but denied the land, or admitted the land but denied the vessels, he is exempt. If he admitted part of the land, he is exempt. If he admitted part of the vessels, he is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא begins a new challenge by quoting a משנה. This step sets up the source, and the next step explains how it attacks the view that הילך is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches that land is not subject to a שבועה. So when the denial is about land, or when the only admission is about land, there is no oath. When he admits part of the vessels and denies the rest of the vessels, he must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: He raises an objection from a source
He claimed from him
Movable vessels and land
He admitted

phrases.aramaic: מֵתִיב מַר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman objected:
If he claimed vessels and land from him,
and he admitted the vessels and denied the land,
or admitted the land and denied the vessels, he is exempt.
If he admitted part of the land, he is exempt.
If he admitted part of the vessels, he is obligated.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב מַר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge, this time against the view that הילך is פטור.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that הילך is פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup: the משנה will be read in the next step to show that a הילך case is חייב.

steps.title: Reading the משנה: הילך is obligated
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה, the גמרא infers that a claim of two sets of vessels, set up like the vessels-and-land case, gives a שבועה. That case must be הילך, so הילך is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason he is exempt is that it was vessels and land, and land is not subject to an oath. But vessels and vessels, set up just like vessels and land, would be obligated. What is the case? Isn't it where he said 'here, take it'? So learn from this that הילך is obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא finishes his challenge. He reads the משנה closely to prove that הילך is חייב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason the vessels-and-land case is exempt is the land. So if the claim were for two sets of vessels, with one admitted and one denied in the same way, there would be a שבועה. The גמרא assumes that this matching case involves the borrower handing over what he admits, which is הילך. That means the משנה rules הילך is חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: Not subject to an oath
Similar to, set up the same way
What is the case?

phrases.english: The reason is that it is vessels and land,
because land is not subject to an oath.
But vessels and vessels,
set up like vessels and land, would be obligated.
What is the case?
Is it not where he said to him, 'Here, take it'?
So learn from it that 'here, take it' is obligated!

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּכֵלִים וְקַרְקָעוֹת, דְּקַרְקַע לָאו בַּת שְׁבוּעָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the משנה quoted in step 14 attacks the view that הילך is פטור.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that הילך is פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה implies that a vessels-and-vessels case is חייב. That case is הילך, so הילך is חייב.
steps.confusionAlert: The משנה itself never mentions הילך. The challenge comes entirely from an inference: what the משנה would rule if land were swapped for vessels.

steps.title: Vessels and vessels is also exempt; the land case teaches something else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference from step 15. A claim of כלים and כלים is also פטור. The משנה chose a case with קרקעות to teach that admitting some of the כלים obligates a שבועה on the land too.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really, I can tell you that a claim of vessels and vessels is also exempt. The משנה gave the case of vessels and land to teach us this: if he admitted part of the vessels, he must swear about the land too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers מר זוטרא's challenge. The משנה's choice of 'vessels and land' was not meant to suggest that 'vessels and vessels' would be different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר זוטרא's proof depended on reading the משנה this way: only land is exempt, so two sets of vessels must be obligated. The גמרא cuts that reading off: both cases are פטור, so there is no proof that הילך is obligated. The land detail was included to teach a new rule: once he must swear about the כלים, he must also swear about the קרקעות he denied.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, I can tell you: the opening of an answer that keeps the original position
This is what it teaches us
Part of the claim
Land, real estate. Normally no שבועה is taken over land.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this answer as saying that land is now generally sworn over. You swear about land only because you already owe a שבועה on the כלים.

phrases.english: No, really I can tell you
vessels and vessels is also exempt,
phrases.notes: This is the case from step 15: a claim of two sets of vessels, set up like the vessels-and-land case.

phrases.english: and the fact that it teaches vessels and land,
this is what it teaches us:
if he admitted part of the vessels,
he is obligated to swear also about the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ כֵּלִים וְכֵלִים נָמֵי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מר זוטרא's inference from the משנה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets why the משנה chose its case: the detail was chosen to teach a different rule, not to set up a contrast.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mention of land implies that vessels and vessels would be obligated, so הילך is obligated.
steps.terutzMaskana: Vessels and vessels is also פטור. The land case teaches that an admission on the כלים brings a שבועה on the קרקעות as well.

steps.title: Why teach this? The rule of binding is already taught elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this new teaching adds. A משנה in קידושין already teaches זוקקין: property without a guarantee pulls in property with a guarantee for a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it teaching us, the rule of binding? We already learned it: property that does not serve as a guarantee binds property that does serve as a guarantee, so he must swear about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 16. If the משנה in שבועות is teaching the binding rule, that seems redundant, because another משנה already says it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes a משנה does not repeat a rule for no reason. The rule step 16 gave is exactly זוקקין, which the משנה in קידושין already states. So the new reason step 16 offered for mentioning land seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Binding: one oath pulls in another claim so that he must swear about it too
We have already learned this in a משנה
Property
Serving as a guarantee for a debt. Land has it; movable things do not.

phrases.english: What is it teaching us, the rule of binding?
We have already learned it:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in קידושין 26a.

phrases.english: property that does not serve as a guarantee binds
phrases.notes: That means movable things, like the vessels.

phrases.english: property that does serve as a guarantee
so that he must swear about it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן – זוֹקְקִין? תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 16 as making the משנה repeat a known rule
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 16's claim that the משנה in שבועות mentions land to teach the binding rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The binding rule is already stated in the משנה in קידושין, so it would be redundant for the משנה in שבועות to come and teach it.

steps.title: This משנה is the rule's main home; the other only mentions it in passing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה in שבועות is the main place for the rule, since it deals with oaths. The משנה in קידושין only brings it up incidentally.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is the main teaching. There, it was brought along in passing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the rule appears twice. Each משנה has a different reason for stating it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה in שבועות, which is about oaths, is the real place for the binding rule. The משנה in קידושין is listing differences between movable property and land, and mentions binding only as part of that list. So step 16's answer holds, and the proof that הילך is obligated falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, meaning the משנה in שבועות
There, meaning the משנה in קידושין
The main place where a rule is taught
Brought along in passing, as part of another topic

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה about כלים and קרקעות does not prove that הילך is obligated. A claim of כלים and כלים is also פטור. Land is mentioned to teach זוקקין, and that rule's main home is the משנה in שבועות.

phrases.english: Here it is the main teaching,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the משנה in שבועות, which is all about oaths.

phrases.english: there, it brought it along in passing.
phrases.notes: 'There' means the משנה in קידושין, which is mainly comparing movable property and land.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא עִיקָּר, הָתָם אַגַּב גְּרָרָא נַסְבַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the redundancy challenge of step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Primary place versus incidental mention: two sources state the same rule for different reasons.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The binding rule is taught twice for no reason.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule's main place is in שבועות. קידושין mentions it only in passing, so there is no redundancy.
